title: Adolescent Sports-Related Lower Extremity Pain and Overuse Injuries.

sections.label: UNLABELED
sections.text: Adolescent participation in organized sports has increased substantially in recent decades, accompanied by a rising incidence of lower extremity pain and overuse injuries. Unique physiologic characteristics of the growing athlete, including open physes and periods of rapid skeletal maturation, combined with early sport specialization and increasing training demands, place adolescents at elevated risk for overuse conditions. This review examines common causes of sports-related lower extremity pain in adolescent athletes, including patellofemoral pain syndrome, Osgood-Schlatter disease, patellar tendinopathy, Sinding-Larsen-Johansson disease, bone stress injuries, and symptomatic flexible flatfoot. For each condition, we review epidemiology, clinical presentation, diagnostic considerations, and contemporary management strategies. Most overuse injuries in this population are diagnosed clinically and respond well to conservative treatment that emphasizes activity modification, progressive rehabilitation, and load management. Imaging should be used judiciously, primarily to confirm diagnosis or exclude alternative pathology. Emerging therapies, including biologic injections and bone stimulation modalities, show promise in select conditions but require further high-quality evidence before routine adoption. Prevention remains central to reducing injury burden. Gradual progression of training load, neuromuscular conditioning, nutritional optimization, and monitoring during growth spurts are key strategies. Increasing evidence also suggests that psychosocial factors may influence injury risk. A multidisciplinary approach involving clinicians, coaches, and strength and conditioning professionals is essential to promote safe, sustainable sports participation and long-term musculoskeletal health in adolescent athletes.
